metadata.file_name: 19. Khoudi et al. (2024). Finding the contextual impacts on Students’ Mathematical performance using a Machine Learning-based Approach.pdf
metadata.title: Finding the contextual impacts on Students’ Mathematical performance using a Machine Learning-based Approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 Morocco grade 8 microdata assembled via IDB Analyzer (version 5.0), combining student, teacher, and school files into a single analytic dataset. The authors explicitly removed variables related to IDs and weights from the explanatory feature pool (e.g., total school weight, total class weight), and they do not report applying any complex survey weights in the ML training/evaluation pipeline. Because the models are standard ML classifiers (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost) trained on a train/test split, the manuscript suggests an unweighted analysis that does not fully account for TIMSS’s clustered sampling design. For preprocessing, they also removed variables with 100% missingness, deleted benchmark/PV-related predictors, filtered variables with >10% missingness, and imputed remaining missing values using SimpleImputer (mode) while retaining all 8390 observations.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is not a TIMSS plausible-value (PV) achievement score; instead, the authors create a binary benchmark-based outcome from TIMSS PV-derived achievement levels using a majority vote across the five PVs (Low vs Others). Because the target is a benchmark classification rather than a PV-based continuous achievement scale, PV handling is not applicable in the sense of PV estimation/combining for the outcome. Missing data handling is reported via SimpleImputer, but the paper does not provide a detailed missingness mechanism assessment; the imputation strategy is therefore treated as a pragmatic preprocessing choice rather than a fully documented PV-aware procedure.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 Morocco grade 8 student data files after combining student, teacher, and school data in IDB Analyzer (v5.0). The authors removed ID/weight/maintenance variables from predictors, deleted variables with 100% missingness, removed numerical scale-score variables that were redundant with categorical indices, removed PVs/benchmark predictors (keeping only the newly generated benchmark variable BSMIBM as the response), and dropped 74 variables with missing rates >10%. They also removed tie cases in the majority-vote benchmark construction (68 ties) and retained the final analytic sample of 8390 students.

main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics achievement (Low vs Others benchmark classification)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SVM — Accuracy: 65.87, F1: 16.03. Random Forest — Accuracy: 79.18, F1: 65.39. XGBoost — Accuracy: 81.92, F1: 74.42.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (Morocco) the study leveraged mathematics achievement too low, classroom libraries, student confidence in mathematics, time spent on math instruction, and work on your own to classify students into Low versus Others. The results found that XGBoost achieved the highest accuracy (81.92) and F1-score (74.42) compared with SVM and Random Forest. This indicates that strengthening classroom learning resources and supporting students’ confidence and independent practice—along with ensuring sufficient instructional time—may improve the proportion of Moroccan students reaching at least the non-Low mathematics benchmark, though the study’s unweighted ML setup and benchmark-based outcome limit causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2019 Morocco grade 8 mathematics using a binary benchmark outcome derived from TIMSS PV-based achievement levels (Low vs Others) and trains three supervised classifiers: SVM, Random Forest, and XGBoost. After preprocessing (removing ID/weight variables, deleting 100% missing predictors, dropping variables with >10% missingness, and imputing remaining missing values with SimpleImputer), the authors split the data into training (n=5873) and test (n=2517) sets with stratification by the response variable. XGBoost performed best, reaching 81.92% accuracy and an F1-score of 74.42, outperforming Random Forest (79.18% accuracy; F1=65.39) and SVM (65.87% accuracy; F1=16.03). Feature importance from XGBoost highlighted 12 contextual factors spanning student confidence, independent work, instructional time, and resource shortages. Limitations include the apparent omission of TIMSS complex survey weights in ML training and the fact that the outcome is a benchmark classification rather than a PV-based continuous score, so results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects.
